films.title: Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, The
films.review: This expansive prequel gives Haymitch’s origins a brutal, emotionally charged backstory, with a strong central performance and an impressive ensemble. Its familiar franchise machinery and overextended plotting can make it feel like another instalment rather than a fresh reinvention, but it remains a substantial, often gripping return to Panem.

films.title: American Doctor
films.review: This harrowing documentary follows three American doctors working in Gaza’s overwhelmed hospitals, then traces their efforts to make the suffering they witnessed heard back home. Its unflinching images are difficult to watch, but the doctors’ commitment and the film’s clear-eyed account of medical work under bombardment give it considerable urgency and emotional force.

films.title: Arthur Christmas (15th Anniversary)
films.synopsis: When Santa's high-tech operation misses one child, his youngest son Arthur sets out on a frantic Christmas Eve mission to deliver the forgotten present before morning.

films.title: Josephine
films.review: A quietly devastating drama about an eight-year-old girl struggling to process a sexual assault she witnesses, anchored by a remarkable performance from young Mason Reeves. Its sensitive attention to the child’s fear and the strain on her family is powerful, though some of the film’s procedural turns and visual choices feel more contrived than convincing.

films.title: A Talent For Murder
films.review: Helen Mirren relishes the role of a fictionalised Patricia Highsmith in this witty, literary chamber thriller, sparring with an ambitious young editor who hopes to coax one last Ripley novel from her. The performances and sharp dialogue make it an enjoyable watch, but its central mystery lacks the menace and tension of Highsmith’s best work.

films.title: Filipinana
films.review: A visually sumptuous, quietly unsettling debut turns an elite Manila golf club into a microcosm of class privilege, exploitation and colonial power. Its deliberate pacing and elusive storytelling demand patience, but the carefully composed images and growing sense of menace give the satire a lasting bite.

films.title: The Match
films.synopsis: A documentary revisits the 1986 Argentina–England World Cup quarter-final, examining how the match became a flashpoint for tensions between the two nations.

films.title: CBeebies Panto 2026: Treasure Island
films.synopsis: A filmed family pantomime follows Jim and his dad Bertie on a swashbuckling treasure hunt, with pirates, songs, comedy and familiar CBeebies performers.

films.title: Heysel 85
films.review: This dramatisation of the 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster gives a tense, human perspective on the chaos surrounding the Liverpool–Juventus European Cup final. Its staging conveys the scale of the tragedy, but a thin script, uneven performances and limited resources struggle to do justice to the historical weight of the events.

films.title: You Can See Everything
films.review: This audacious documentary-hybrid turns the story of Elizabeth Holmes into a gripping, often surreal study of performance, deception and the manufacture of reality. Nathan Fielder’s unsettling methods and the film’s unexpected shifts make it as provocative as it is entertaining, although its deliberate blurring of fact and fiction leaves plenty of questions hanging.

films.title: Steps
films.review: This lively Cinderella reworking gives the supposedly wicked stepsisters their own story, with spirited voice performances and enough comic energy to keep the adventure moving. The plot becomes crowded with subplots and familiar fairytale reversals, while the animation lacks a distinctive look, but its humour and pace make it a cheerful family diversion.

films.title: Sathyavan Savithri
films.synopsis: A young lawyer takes on the case of her husband, whom she believes has been wrongly convicted of murder, and finds herself opposed in court by her own mentor.

films.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
films.review: Mahershala Ali gives a deeply felt performance as a widowed Muslim hitman trying to reconcile his violent work with the demands of fatherhood and faith. The film’s vivid, often brutal action is matched by an unexpectedly tender family drama, though its deliberately strange tone and crowded religious themes make for an unsettling rather than straightforwardly entertaining experience.

films.title: 70 Syaal
films.synopsis: A man returns with his family to his ancestral village in Punjab to bring peace to his dying father, but their homecoming awakens a decades-old supernatural curse that threatens his wife and newborn child.
